rationale: The static profile is empty (no source lines, function list, or sizes), so the table is calibrated to what is known about this sample: ffbench is a tiny SingleSource/Misc benchmark dominated by one or two hot floating-point kernels, meaning nearly all execution time concentrates in a very small amount of code and any per-instruction overhead in those loops is paid thousands of times over. I therefore prioritize cheap, universally applicable transformations and de-emphasize expensive control-flow rewrites: SUB gets the highest SecurityGain weight because instruction substitution is lightweight, blends naturally with FP-heavy arithmetic, and carries negligible runtime/size cost, so it can be applied aggressively everywhere including hot loops. BCF and FLA are kept at moderate security weights but with low RuntimeCost weights, signaling the selector should only fire them on cold or lightly-executed functions where their heavy dispatch-loop and bogus-predicate overhead is amortized; flattening the hot kernel would tank the benchmark's runtime. SPLIT is heavily weighted toward RuntimeCost/SizeCost being acceptable and CorrectnessRisk being tolerable because splitting basic blocks is nearly free and increases the granularity other passes (FLA, BCF, IBR) operate on, so it should run broadly as an enabler. IBR gets strong weights across runtime and correctness tolerance since indirect branching is cheap relative to its real-analysis value in a control-flow-dense kernel, and ICALL is moderately enabled to convert direct calls into indirect ones — effective against static call-graph recovery with only small call overhead in a program that makes few calls. IGV is weakest: global variable indirection matters more for programs with rich state, and this sample's profile gives no evidence of globals worth hiding, so it is allowed but only at low priority. Overall the table biases the selector toward low-cost arithmetic/structure passes on hot code and reserves the expensive passes for cold regions, keeping overhead acceptable while maximizing resistance for a tiny, latency-sensitive numeric workload.
